yes adverb

also yeah, yep, yes, I did, yes, it is, yes, I do, I say yes, you say no, by all means!, rather!, I should say so!

classical

Ter. And. 849b–850: Mihine? — Ita.
Hor. S. 2.7.2: Dāvusne? — ita, Dāvus
Traupman 250: ita and sīc mean “it is so”
Traupman 250, 410

ita

adverb · Wiktionary

yes (it is so)

The plainest yes; stronger, ita vērō, ita prōrsus (Lewis & Short). Most often, though, Latin answers with no particle at all: it repeats the word the question turns on (Traupman 250), Vēnitne? — Vēnit. (Plaut. Bacch. 247).

Other words

  • etiam — yes (indeed)

    adverb · also used · classical · Plaut. Amph. 544–544b: numquid vīs? — Etiam: ut āctūtum adveniās.; Cic. Ac. 2.104: aut etiam aut nōn respondēre possit; Traupman 67, 410 · Wiktionary

    Cicero’s word for the bare yes of a yes-or-no answer.

  • sānē — yes, certainly, by all means

    adverb · also used · classical · Plaut. Ps. 664–664b: Quīn ubi pranderō, dabō operam somnō. — Sānē cēnseō.; Plaut. Poen. 1079–1079b: sed tē monērī num nevīs? — Sānē volō.; Traupman 288; Traupman 68, 410 · Wiktionary

    The yes that grants or approves: “yes, do”, “yes, I’d like that”.

  • maximē — yes, certainly (willing assent)

    adverb · also used · classical · Ter. Ad. 609b–609c: Sequere mē ergō hāc intrō. — Maximē.; Plaut. Most. 1009–1009b: operam mihi dā. — Maximē.; Traupman 103: by all means!, maximē! · Wiktionary

    (in this sense, vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Plaut., Ter.)

    The willing yes to a request or an order; its pair is Minimē!, not at all (see no way!).

  • admodum — yes, quite so

    adverb · also used · classical · Ter. Hec. 458–458b: Advenīs modo? — Admodum.; Cic. Leg. 3.26 (Lewis & Short) · Wiktionary

    (in this sense, vōx cōmica: often in Plautus, twice in Terence)

    Cicero names Admodum and Prōrsus ita est as the yeses said in conversation to let it move on (Leg. 3.26, quoted by Lewis & Short).

  • sīc — yes, so it is

    also used · classical · Ter. Ph. 2.2.2: Phaniam relictam ais? — Sīc. (Lewis & Short); Traupman 250 · Wiktionary

    (vōx cōmica: Ter.; rāra)

    Lewis & Short: “in answers, yes = the French, Italian, and Spanish sì (ante-class. and rare)”.

  • plānē — yes, exactly so

    also used · classical · Plaut. Truc. 2.7.57: Plānē istuc est. (Lewis & Short); Traupman 250 · Wiktionary

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut.)

    Lewis & Short: “in affirmative answers, certainly, to be sure, exactly so (ante-class.)”. Traupman 250 also lists certē, oppidō and plānissimē; Lewis & Short gives oppidō as a colloquial “very, exactly” and no instance of it, or of plānissimē, as an answer.

Examples

  • Quid ais? an vēnit Pamphilus? — Vēnit. — Dīs grātiam habeō.

    What did you say? Has Pamphilus come? — He has. — Thank the gods.Ter. Hec. 346–346c

  • quid istīc tibi negōtī est? — Mihine? — Ita.

    What business have you in there? — Me? — Yes, you.Ter. And. 849–850

  • Quīn ubi pranderō, dabō operam somnō. — Sānē cēnseō.

    After lunch I’ll have a nap. — Yes, do.Plaut. Ps. 664–664b

  • Tū, Parmenō, hūc fac illī addūcantur. — Maximē.

    “Parmeno, see that they are brought here.” “Certainly.”Ter. Eun. 189

  • Negat quis? negō. Ait? ajō.

    Someone says no? I say no. Says yes? I say yes.Ter. Eun. 2.2.21 (Lewis & Short s.v. ajō)

  • Ego ajō, tū negās.

    I say yes, you say no.Traupman 112

  • Hunc nōvistī? — Facile!

    Do you know this fellow? — Rather!Traupman 106

  • Ego ajō; tū negās.

    I say yes; you say no.Traupman 410

See also that’s right, no way!, of course, agree, allow, do.
